outputs.L3:
A woman’s death, at first presented as a hanging, soon begins to look far more like murder. Her body bears signs that do not fit a simple suicide: bruises on her skin, a neck twisted in a way that suggests violence, and a scene surrounded by troubling inconsistencies. The circumstances raise suspicion among those who knew her, leaving the community uneasy and fearful that something darker than grief is at work.

In the aftermath, rumors spread of a threatening figure—perhaps a spirit, perhaps something even more dangerous—appearing to the woman’s new man. This presence is said to have warned him that he would be next, turning a private tragedy into a wider terror. The warning suggests that the woman’s death may not be the end of the violence, but the beginning of a chain of events driven by revenge, guilt, or an evil force that has attached itself to the living.

The narrator also encounters this supernatural presence. It is not fully human, but something shifting and unnatural: a vapor-like form that laughs in the darkness. Its laughter carries menace, as though it takes pleasure in fear and suffering. Whether it is the dead woman returning, a spirit using her death as a doorway, or some older haunting force, the apparition makes it clear that the boundary between the living and the dead has been disturbed.

The community’s suffering deepens when another tragedy strikes. Three brothers are killed in a car wreck on ice, their deaths adding to the sense that misfortune is spreading through the area. What might have been dismissed as coincidence begins to feel like a pattern. Fear settles over the people, and the earlier suspicions surrounding the woman’s death grow into a belief that an evil presence is moving among them.

In response, the people prepare to fight back in the only ways they know: through prayer, ritual, and collective faith. They gather themselves against the darkness, hoping that spiritual strength can protect them where ordinary means have failed. At the same time, the brother appears destined for a direct confrontation with the force, one that will lead him to the river. There, the struggle between the living and the haunting presence seems likely to reach its final and dangerous test.
outputs.L4:
A haunted community is thrown into fear after a woman is found dead in what first appears to be a hanging. At a glance, the death might be taken for suicide, but the details surrounding the body suggest something far more sinister. There are marks and signs that point toward violence, as if the woman was not merely taken by despair but attacked, overpowered, and murdered. Her death becomes the beginning of a larger mystery, one that the people around her struggle to understand through eyewitness testimony, rumor, grief, and spiritual belief.

As the community tries to make sense of what has happened, different accounts begin to form a disturbing pattern. Witnesses describe strange presences, unnatural movements, and a force that does not behave like an ordinary human killer. The deaths are not isolated accidents; they seem connected by something unseen, something that moves like vapor or smoke and carries with it the threat of further violence. The atmosphere becomes one of dread, as if the living are being watched by a malevolent power that can enter their world at any moment.

In response, the people turn not only to reason but also to ritual. Bells are rung, prayers are spoken, and spiritual practices are used as a form of resistance against the evil that has entered their lives. These acts are not merely symbolic. For the frightened community, the bell and the prayer become weapons of protection, ways of naming and confronting a force that cannot easily be touched or understood. Faith, memory, and communal action become their means of survival.

At the center of this terror is the dead woman’s brother, whose grief hardens into determination. He recognizes that the force behind the deaths is not finished and that more lives may be lost if no one acts. His decision to drag the malevolent presence into the river is both desperate and meaningful. It is an act of vengeance for his sister, but also an act of protection for the community. By confronting the vaporous evil directly, he attempts to break its power, contain its violence, and prevent the haunting from claiming anyone else. The moment stands as a grim but significant gesture of courage in the face of an enemy that is terrifying precisely because it exists between the physical and the spiritual worlds.
outputs.L5:
The man stood beneath the old streetlight, waiting for her.

The night was quiet, filled only with the soft sound of wind moving through the trees. He held a small letter in his hand, folded carefully at the edges. It was from her—the one person who had changed the way he saw the world.

The man had never believed that a single moment could alter an entire life, but meeting her had done exactly that. Her kindness, her laughter, and the strength in her eyes stayed with him wherever he went.

The letter contained only a few words, but they were enough:

“Meet me where the story began.”

So he waited, remembering the day they first spoke, the promises they made, and the dreams they once shared. And when he finally saw her walking toward him through the golden glow of the light, the man smiled.

The story was not over.

It was only beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal gothic horror passage about a murdered woman hanging from a tree, a vengeful spirit, brothers dying in an icy car wreck, and a man preparing to fight the demon with prayer and bells.
counterfactuals.output:
The woman hung from the black yew as though the tree had dreamed her there.

All night the branches creaked above the old road, though there was no wind, and the moon lay broken in the ditch-water like a drowned saint’s face. Her white dress had gone gray with frost. Her hair trailed downward in wet ropes, brushing the bark, and from the place where her shadow touched the snow, nothing living would cross—not fox, not crow, not the pale village dogs that came to the cemetery gate and whimpered until dawn.

They had buried her once.

They had buried her with a hymn trembling on every tongue and lies folded neatly beneath the coffin lid. But the earth would not keep her. By the third midnight, the grave had opened like an eye, and by morning she was hanging again from the yew, swaying gently over the road where her murderer had last kissed her hands and called it love.

After that, the bells in the church tower began ringing by themselves.

Not loudly. Never loudly. Only one slow note at a time, deep as a heart heard through soil.

The first brother died on a road glazed silver with ice. He had been laughing, they said, drunk on grief and brandy, driving too fast past the yew where the dead woman turned her head to watch. His motorcar slid without sound. It struck the bridge wall and folded inward like a prayer book slammed shut.

The second brother came to identify the body. He swore at the corpse, at the road, at the tree. He swore he saw a woman in the rear window of the wreck, seated primly in the frost, her face hidden by a veil of hair. That night, he too took the bridge too quickly. The river below was frozen hard enough to hold a man’s weight, but not his sins. They found the car upside down in the reeds, its wheels spinning lazily in the moonlight, its horn bleating until sunrise like an animal caught in a trap.

By then, everyone knew she was not alone.

Something had climbed out with her.

Something older than her grief had found a doorway in the violence done beneath the yew. It wore her sorrow like a bridal veil. It borrowed her dangling feet, her bruised throat, the soft tilt of her murdered head. But when it smiled, the villagers saw teeth where no human mouth should have been, and when it spoke from the branches, it spoke in many voices—brothers, fathers, sons, all choking on winter.

Only Father Callum remained in the chapel after the others fled.

He barred the doors at dusk and laid his weapons across the altar: a rosary blackened by years of fingers, a silver handbell, a brass bell from the abandoned schoolhouse, and the great rope that rang the tower bell above. He lit twelve candles, though thirteen flames appeared. He opened the old prayer book to pages stiff with candle wax and grave damp, and he marked his brow with ash from last Easter’s palms.

Outside, the yew tapped one branch against the stained-glass window.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

Like a fingernail on a coffin lid.

Father Callum did not look up.

He wrapped the rosary around his wrist until the beads bit into his skin. He took the silver bell in his left hand and the brass bell in his right. Above him, the tower bell began to swing on its own, slow and hungry, answering a rhythm no living hand had made.

In the nave, the shadows lengthened.

At the door, something breathed through the keyhole.

And from the road came the faint, impossible sound of a woman laughing beneath a tree, while dead brothers called from the ice, begging to be let in.

Father Callum raised the bells.

“Not tonight,” he whispered.

Then he began to pray.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a disturbing, dreamlike paragraph in the style of a badly translated 19th-century ghost story involving murder, a river, archangels, a laughing apparition, and foreshadowed deaths.
counterfactuals.output: At the black hour when the moon hung like a sick plate above the river, Sir Adalbert came walking with the knife yet warm in his glove, and behind him the water spoke in small drowned syllables, as if it was rehearsing names. Upon the bridge stood three archangels, very tall and incorrectly made, their wings folded like wet maps, and they regarded him with the sorrowful politeness of judges who have already eaten. Then from beneath the planks arose the apparition of the murdered bride, her throat smiling wider than her mouth, and she laughed—O, how she laughed!—not with merriment but with the clattering sound of tea-cups in a sealed room. “Go home, my husband,” she said, though he had never married her, “for the bed is dug, the candles are thirsty, and before the cock remembers morning, your brother shall fall from the west stair, your mother shall drink the mirror, and you shall enter the river by your own hand, thinking it a door.” Sir Adalbert fled, but the archangels followed without walking, and the river below turned over in its sleep, showing for one instant the pale faces of all who were not yet dead.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an AI-written horror excerpt with fragmented grammar and biblical imagery: a woman is found dead, her ghost returns, more brothers die, and the narrator vows to drag the damned spirit into the river.
counterfactuals.output:
They found Mara under the sycamore. Mouth full of black rain. Hair spread like a torn veil. Her hands folded upon her breast, prayer-like, but wrong. Too tight. As if she had been holding the name of God and crushed it.

No one spoke.

The moon hung over us, pale as a communion wafer. The river moved beyond the reeds, whispering scripture in a drowned man’s tongue.

Three nights after we buried her, she came back.

Not walking. Not breathing. Just there, in the doorway of our father’s house, dripping mud and grave-water onto the threshold. Her eyes were lamps with no flame. Her lips blue. Her voice—when it came—was my mother’s voice, and not my mother’s voice, saying, *Brother.*

Elias answered first.

By dawn, he was hanging from the rafters, tongue black, feet bare, Bible open beneath him to the plagues of Egypt.

Then Jonah.

Found in the well, face turned upward, smiling like he had seen angels, though his nails were gone and his chest was marked with finger-burns.

Then little Samuel, sweet Samuel, who had never harmed so much as a field mouse. He heard her singing from the orchard. We heard him laughing. We found only his coat, laid neatly across a stump, and a trail of wet footprints leading back to Mara’s grave.

Mother said it was punishment. Father said nothing. Sat at the table with ash on his head, like Job among the ruins.

But I know what she is.

Not sister. Not saint. Not lamb returned to the fold.

She is the thing that wore Mara’s grief until grief became teeth. She is the worm in the psalm. The bride of the pit. The pale rider’s handmaiden, come to reap our house down to dust.

Tonight I go to the river.

I have salt. Iron. A rope knotted seven times. My father’s knife. The old hymn carved into my palm where blood can remember what the tongue forgets.

Let her come.

Let her stand among the reeds in her burial dress, dripping and holy and ruined. Let her call me *Brother* with that dead-soft mouth.

I will answer.

I will bind her by the hair. By the bones. By the name she stole from the living.

And if Heaven will not take her, and Hell has left her loose upon the earth, then I will drag that damned spirit down into the river myself, and hold her there until the water learns to pray.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange supernatural murder scene where bruises reveal foul play, a vaporous figure laughs “Ha Ha, Goody!”, and the surviving brother must battle an insidious soul using faith.
counterfactuals.output:
By the time the minister arrived, the snow had stopped falling and the house had gone silent in that peculiar way houses do when they are ashamed.

It stood at the edge of the orchard, its windows filmed white with frost, its chimney breathing no smoke. Inside, the parlor smelled of cold ashes, tallow, and something wet underneath the floorboards. The candles on the mantel burned with blue points, though no one had lit them, and their flames bent as if listening.

Abel Merrit lay on his back before the hearth.

At first glance it might have been said he had died in sleep and fallen from his chair. His Bible lay open beside him, its pages ruffled by no wind. His face was peaceful enough, save for the dark crescent under his lower lip and the unnatural stillness of his eyes, which seemed fixed upon some terror above the rafters.

But then his brother Samuel saw the wrists.

“Hold the light nearer,” he whispered.

The constable lowered the lantern.

Around both of Abel’s wrists were bruises—four long marks on each side, deep and purple, as though fingers had clamped there with terrible patience. More bruises laddered up his arms: small, round, spiteful blooms beneath the skin. At his throat, just above the collar, was the print of a thumb.

“No man did that,” the constable said, though the words seemed to pain him.

Samuel knelt, trembling. He had not wept yet. Grief stood somewhere behind the shock, waiting its turn.

Abel’s mouth opened.

Everyone in the room lurched back.

From between the dead man’s teeth leaked a ribbon of gray vapor. It uncurled slowly, like breath on a winter morning, but there was no warmth in it. The vapor rose, thickened, and gathered itself into the faint shape of a woman: hunched shoulders, a narrow head in a bonnet, hands hooked like claws. Her face was not a face, only a suggestion of eyes and a hole for a mouth.

Then the thing laughed.

“Ha Ha, Goody!”

The sound clattered around the parlor like stones in a pan.

The minister crossed himself before remembering he was not of that church. The constable dropped the lantern, and its glass cracked, spilling light crookedly across the floor.

Samuel did not move.

The vaporous woman bent over him until the air around his face became cold enough to sting.

“Brother left,” she hissed, though her mouth hardly formed the words. “Brother living. Brother warm.”

Samuel knew then what had worn Abel’s flesh down from the inside these past weeks. It had not been fever. It had not been melancholy. Abel had complained of dreams in which an old woman sat upon his chest and whispered his childhood sins into his ear. He had shown Samuel the bruises once, laughing weakly, saying he must have struck himself in sleep.

Now the bruises had told the truth.

The thing that had murdered Abel had not finished feeding.

The candles guttered out all at once.

Darkness crashed into the room.

In it, Samuel heard the dead boards creak under invisible weight. He heard Abel’s corpse give a small, obscene sigh. Then something slipped into him—not through his mouth or nose, but through memory. It entered by way of guilt.

He saw Abel at ten years old, falling through the ice while Samuel ran for help.

He saw Abel at twenty, taking blame for a theft Samuel had committed.

He saw Abel yesterday, pale and begging him to stay the night, while Samuel, irritated and proud, had gone home.

The insidious soul pressed against Samuel’s own, smooth and patient as a hand over a flame.

You left him.

Samuel staggered. His knees struck the floorboards.

You will carry me better.

His breath shortened. His fingers curled against his will. He felt hatred rise in him—hatred for the minister, for the constable, for Abel lying useless and dead, for God Himself, who had permitted the room to become a den of old darkness.

The minister shouted something, but Samuel heard only the woman’s laughter inside his skull.

“Ha Ha, Goody! Ha Ha, Goody!”

Then his hand touched the open Bible.

The page had been marked with Abel’s blood, one thumbprint smeared beside the line: *Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.*

Samuel clutched the book as if it were a ledge above a pit.

“No,” he said.

The thing inside him tightened.

Samuel’s voice broke. “No.”

He dragged the Bible to his chest and forced himself to speak, though every word burned. He did not speak prettily. He did not sound like the minister on Sabbath morning. He sounded like a frightened man in a murdered house, using faith as a blade because nothing else would cut.

“The Lord is my shepherd,” Samuel gasped. “I shall not want.”

The room bucked.

Frost raced across the walls. The shadow of the vapor-woman stretched long and crooked over the ceiling, though no light remained to cast it.

“He maketh me to lie down in green pastures—”

Liar, the soul whispered. Coward. Bad brother. Weak brother.

Samuel wept at last, tears hot on his face. “He restoreth my soul.”

At that, the thing shrieked.

Not aloud. Worse—within him. Its scream tore through every hidden chamber of his heart, clawing at old shame, old bitterness, old fear. Samuel felt his body arch backward. He saw, dimly, the minister and constable holding him down. He saw Abel’s corpse jerk once, as though some thread tied between them had been pulled taut.

Samuel pressed the Bible harder to his chest.

“Though I walk,” he said, each word a nail driven into a coffin lid, “through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.”

The vapor-woman appeared before him again, forced outward from his body by inches. Her faceless head writhed. Her fingers smoked where they touched the holy book.

“For Thou art with me,” Samuel said.

The parlor filled with a sound like a thousand wings beating behind stone.

“Thy rod and Thy staff, they comfort me.”

The thing tried once more to laugh, but the laugh broke apart.

“Ha—Ha—Goo—”

Samuel opened his eyes and looked directly into the hollow where its face should have been.

“You cannot have him,” he said. “And you cannot have me.”

The last candle on the mantel flared white.

The vapor-woman was pulled upward like smoke into a chimney, twisting, thinning, shrieking until she became no more than a stain on the air. Then even that vanished.

Silence returned.

This time it was clean.

Samuel collapsed beside his brother’s body. The bruises on Abel’s wrists had darkened almost black, final testimony beneath the skin. Foul play, yes—but not of any earthly hand.

At dawn, when they carried Abel out, the snow beneath the threshold had melted in the shape of two bare feet facing inward.

No tracks led away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a dark, incoherent folklore-style narrative about a haunted hanging, no footprints at the crime scene, a demon enticing women to death, and a fisherman-brother confronting evil in a boiling river.
counterfactuals.output:
They say it happened in the parish where the trees leaned away from the church and the crows would not roost after sunset.

A woman was found hanging from the old gallows-ash, though no rope had been taken from any barn and no ladder stood beneath her. Her feet were clean. The mud below was clean. All around the tree the earth lay smooth as butter, without heel, toe, claw, or drag-mark, though rain had fallen all night and every honest creature left its signature in the lane.

The villagers crossed themselves and said she had walked there in the air.

But old Mara, who had three teeth and remembered too much, said no, she had been called.

For in those days a thing lived near the river, wearing the voice of a lover and the eyes of a drowned saint. It came at windows after midnight and whispered to women who were lonely, women who were grieving, women who had lost children or husbands or names. It promised them a green country under the water, a bed of rushes, a crown of minnows, a mother’s arms, a bridegroom’s kiss.

“Come down,” it sang. “Come down, pretty lamb. There is no sorrow where the river keeps its wives.”

One by one they went.

Some were found in reeds, smiling blue. Some were found hanging from branches too thin to hold a cat. Some were never found, except in dreams, combing their hair with fishbones and laughing backward.

The woman on the gallows-ash had a brother, a fisherman named Ivo, whose nets always came up full until the day she died. After that, his nets rose empty but warm, and sometimes they held black hair knotted with weeds, and sometimes a white hand would grip the mesh from below and let go before he could scream.

Ivo swore by salt, iron, and the cracked bell of Saint Oran that he would take the demon’s tongue.

At moonrise he went to the river with a hook made from his sister’s wedding pin and a line braided from her burial shroud. The river was not running that night. It was boiling. Great bubbles rose and burst with voices inside them—women crying, women singing, women calling him brother, husband, son.

Then the thing came up.

It had antlers of bone and a woman’s mouth. It wore his sister’s face badly, as a thief wears a stolen coat. Its eyes were lamps under ice.

“Dear Ivo,” it said, “your sister is happy. She hangs no more. She dances below. Come see.”

The river boiled higher. Fish burst open in the foam. The moon turned red as a butcher’s thumb.

Ivo cast the hook.

The demon laughed and opened its many mouths, and from each mouth spoke a woman’s last word. One said “mercy.” One said “mother.” One said his sister’s name, though names are not to be trusted on cursed water.

The hook caught in the demon’s tongue.

Then all the hanged women stood up from the river.

Not alive, no. Not dead either. Their hair streamed upward like weeds in a wrong current, and their feet did not touch mud, and there were still no footprints anywhere, only steam and the smell of old rope.

They pulled.

Ivo pulled.

The demon thrashed until the river boiled white and the stones cracked with heat. It promised Ivo gold. It promised him his sister breathing. It promised him a boat that would never sink and a grave that would never open.

He said nothing, for fishermen know that answering a river is how it learns your weight.

At last the tongue tore free.

The scream went into the hills and soured the milk in every cow by morning. The gallows-ash split down its trunk. The river stopped boiling and ran black to the sea, carrying with it antlers, hair, teeth, and the shadows of women who had not cast shadows in years.

Ivo brought the tongue to the church and nailed it under the altar stone, where it wriggled for seven days and whispered for seven nights.

After that, no woman was called from her bed.

But on certain evenings, when the fog lies low and the mud is soft, people still find the old hanging tree circled by perfect, untouched earth.

No footprints going in.

No footprints going out.

And if a girl hears someone singing from the river, sweet as a remembered kiss, her mother spits into the fire and says:

“Stuff your ears, child. Evil does not always come walking.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
